episodes.title: Killing of Joe Burnes
episodes.summary: The killing of Joe Burnes was the fatal shooting of a Black barber by a police officer in Kansas City, Missouri, reported in a wire dispatch dated January 2, 1882. Officer Lovett, who was said to have mistaken Burnes for a thief, shot him dead when he did not stop, and Lovett was reported exonerated. The item ran as a single paragraph of telegraph news in papers from Texas to Washington.

episodes.title: Assault on Ike Johnson
episodes.summary: The assault on Ike Johnson was a roadside attack on a Black man and his wife by two armed white men near the northern edge of Austin, Texas, on the night of January 2, 1882. When Officer J. L. Watts tried to arrest the two men at a house of ill fame later that night, one of them, Emmet McPhail, was shot dead and the other, Jeff Ake, wounded Watts. Papers outside Austin reported the episode as the killing of an ex-convict, and the attack on Johnson was described in detail mainly in the Austin Statesman's inquest coverage.

episodes.title: Hickory church burning
episodes.summary: The Hickory church burning was a night attack at Hickory, Mississippi, in which a Black church was fired into and burned and the town calaboose was burned, around the turn of 1881–82. Three white men and a Black man were arrested on the charges, and a judge went to the town to investigate. The one surviving report, from the Brandon Republican, described a community stirred by lawlessness that its officials had failed to stop.

episodes.title: Lynching of Henry Solomon
episodes.summary: The lynching of Henry Solomon took place at the Bossier parish jail in Bellevue, Louisiana, in the early hours of January 25, 1882, when ten or twelve unknown men took the jail keys from a deputy sheriff and hanged Solomon, a Black prisoner held on a charge of mule stealing. Hours earlier, by the deputy's account, Solomon had set his cell on fire in an attempt to escape. A coroner's jury found that he died by hanging at the hands of 'parties unknown,' and a Louisiana editor later held up the case as evidence that lynchers spared white criminals.

episodes.title: False report of the lynching of Calvin Luckey
episodes.summary: The false report of the lynching of Calvin Luckey was a January 1882 newspaper story that a mob in Randolph County, West Virginia, had hanged a Black man named Luckey after he shot the white father of the woman he had married. First printed by the Wheeling Register and copied by papers from Virginia to Dakota, the story was called a lie by the Randolph County press within a week. Papers that had carried it then retracted it as 'wholly untrue' or contradicted it.

episodes.title: Shooting of Dick Milner
episodes.summary: The shooting of Dick Milner took place in Hickman, Kentucky, probably on Monday, January 30, 1882, when City Marshal Barnes shot Milner, a Black man, in the leg as he ran from arrest. The wound was reported as not dangerous, and the only known account is a brief item in the local Hickman Courier.

episodes.title: Police shooting of Smith in San Antonio
episodes.summary: The police shooting of Smith in San Antonio took place on the morning of January 7, 1882, when Policeman Martinez shot a Black man named Smith in the hip while arresting him as a suspected robber. Smith survived with a flesh wound and was jailed. The case drew a local editorial in the San Antonio Evening Light that criticized arming the police and said Martinez faced a charge of assault with intent to murder.

episodes.title: Threatened lynching of Jake Lewis and others at Graball, Texas
episodes.summary: The threatened lynching of Jake Lewis and others at Graball, Texas, was a reported threat by local citizens in January 1882 against Black men arrested for the murder and beheading of Jordan Thompson, a Black man. No lynching took place; Lewis pleaded guilty, was held in jail, and in April was convicted of manslaughter and sentenced to twenty years. The threat is known only from a telegraphic brief, while the local paper described an excited crowd held back from the courthouse by guards.

episodes.title: Killing of Marshal Smith
episodes.summary: The killing of Marshal Smith was the fatal shooting of a Black preacher at his door on Carruthers' plantation at Clinton, Louisiana, on a Thursday night in late January 1882. Two white men, named in the dispatches as McKee and Singlebarre or Singlebury, were arrested for the murder on circumstantial evidence. The case reached the national press only as a brief wire item, and no later report of its outcome was found.

episodes.title: Threatened lynching of Lincoln County arson suspects (1882)
episodes.summary: The threatened lynching of Lincoln County arson suspects took place in January 1882 in Lincoln County, Georgia, where Black men jailed on an accusation of trying to burn the house of P. A. Cox near Lincolnton were threatened with lynching. County officials kept the prisoners from the threatened lynching, though an Augusta dispatch said fear for their lives persisted.

episodes.title: Beating of Jim Dunlap aboard the steamer James Lee
episodes.summary: The beating of Jim Dunlap aboard the steamer James Lee took place near Memphis, Tennessee, on the night of February 7, 1882, when the boat's crew attacked Dunlap, a Black deck passenger they accused of pushing the second mate overboard. He was beaten so badly that his life was despaired of before the boat's officers could reach him. The episode survives only as a short wire paragraph reprinted in small-town papers across several states.

episodes.title: Attempted lynching of William Medley
episodes.summary: The attempted lynching of William Medley took place in the Bear Quarter section of Norfolk County, Virginia, on about February 10, 1882, when residents tried to lynch a Black man accused of assaulting a five-year-old girl. Constable David Sykes got him to jail, and a Norfolk dispatch noted that the angry residents included both whites and Black people. Medley was later tried in the county court and sentenced to twenty years in the penitentiary.

episodes.title: Attempted lynching of "Majah" Alford
episodes.summary: The attempted lynching of "Majah" Alford took place on Sunday, February 12, 1882, when a crowd of about fifty went to the jail at Gainesville, Texas, intending to seize Alford, a Black music teacher accused of attempting to rape a fourteen-year-old girl. The crowd confined itself to talk and threats and withdrew when the jail guards refused it, and Alford remained in custody to await trial. The episode is known from a single item in the Waco Daily Examiner, which quoted the Gainesville Hesperian.

episodes.title: Nashville police shooting of a fleeing Black man (1882)
episodes.summary: The Nashville police shooting of a fleeing Black man took place in Nashville, Tennessee, on a Tuesday in mid-February 1882, apparently February 14, when a policeman fired at a man running from him. The bullet missed, and no one was hurt. The Memphis Daily Appeal noted the incident chiefly to remark that an officer who killed a fleeing person who was not a felon could be prosecuted for murder.

episodes.title: Attempted lynching of James Redden
episodes.doubt: the local paper denied any attempt; Wilmington reports called sensational
episodes.summary: The attempted lynching of James Redden was a reported effort by residents of the Odessa and Middletown area of New Castle County, Delaware, to lynch Redden, a Black man accused of raping a young girl, on 24–25 February 1882. Wilmington dispatches said officers resisted an organized attempt and took him safely to New Castle jail, but the local Middletown Transcript denied that any attempt was made. Redden was later tried, convicted of rape and hanged at New Castle on 25 August 1882.

episodes.title: Masked raid on Berry Lawrence's house
episodes.summary: The masked raid on Berry Lawrence's house was a night attack by four masked men on the home of a Black man near Cuthbert, Randolph County, Georgia, on Tuesday, 28 February 1882. Lawrence shot the first raider through the broken door, and the dead man was unmasked as Leonidas Bailey, a young white man of the county. A coroner's jury called the killing justifiable homicide, and the wire story of a Black householder killing a masked white raider ran in papers from Washington to Texas.

episodes.title: Centreville roadside ambush
episodes.summary: The Centreville roadside ambush was a shooting near Centreville, Texas, in February 1882, in which a white man named Lyle fired from hiding on two Black men named Hall and their wives as they rode in a wagon. Both men were killed and both women were reported mortally wounded. Carried by a St. Louis telegraph dispatch, the story ran in papers from West Virginia to California under headlines such as "Negroes Waylaid and Shot" and "Double Murder."

episodes.title: Watertown posse pursuit of a Black barber (1882)
episodes.summary: The Watertown posse pursuit of a Black barber was a manhunt in Watertown, apparently in Dakota Territory, reported in February 1882, in which a citizens' posse pursued an unnamed Black barber accused of attempting to rape a local woman. The single report said that he would be dealt with summarily if caught, but it gave no outcome, and no later report was found.

episodes.title: Killing of Robert Taylor in the Maryland Penitentiary
episodes.summary: The killing of Robert Taylor took place on the afternoon of March 1, 1882, when James Byrne, an officer of the Maryland penitentiary in Baltimore, shot dead Taylor, a Black convict, in the prison foundry. A coroner's jury ruled the same day that Byrne had acted in self-defense, and the story ran in short wire items as the shooting of an insubordinate convict.

episodes.title: Attempted lynching of Jack and Manuel Brown
episodes.summary: The attempted lynching of Jack and Manuel Brown was an unsuccessful attempt, on the night of March 1, 1882, at Lexington, Mississippi, to lynch two young Black men charged with attacking the storekeeper A. H. Pinkston. The attempt failed, and the only report of it was a single sentence in a Mississippi weekly's column of state news.

episodes.title: Lynching of Bob Sarver
episodes.summary: The lynching of Bob Sarver was the hanging of a young Black man by a mob near Franklin, Simpson County, Kentucky, on the night of Monday, March 6, 1882. Accused of attempting to rape a 16-year-old white girl, Sarver was taken from officers who were moving him by train and was hanged from a tree at the scene of the alleged attempt. A one-line Nashville dispatch carried the case to papers across the country, and three men were later reported arrested for the killing.

episodes.title: Lynching of John Redmond, Charles Shelton and Harry French
episodes.summary: The lynching of John Redmond, Charles Shelton and Harry French took place at Los Lunas, New Mexico, in early March 1882, when masked men took the three prisoners from the jail and hanged them from the nearest trees. The same mob took two Black prisoners from the jail, beat them and turned them loose. The story spread nationwide through an Albuquerque special to the Denver Republican, which presented the three hanged men as murderers.

episodes.title: Third Creek riot
episodes.summary: The Third Creek riot was a fight between whites and Black men at Third Creek station on the Western North Carolina Railroad on Saturday, March 11, 1882. About a hundred people took part, some with pistols and shotguns, and several Black men were badly but not fatally shot. A Salisbury militia company ended the fighting and jailed twenty-four rioters, and a Raleigh dispatch carried the story to papers across the country under headlines such as "Negroes Rioting in North Carolina."

episodes.title: Burning of Isham Edwards's fence and mule
episodes.summary: The burning of Isham Edwards's fence and mule was a pair of night-time attacks in March 1882 on the farm of Isham Edwards, a Black tenant on the Papy place, six miles from Tallahassee, Florida. Unidentified attackers burned about fifty panels of his fence on 11 March and the next night set his mule on fire in its stable, injuring the animal badly. The Weekly Floridian of Tallahassee condemned the attack on the mule as "fiendish cruelty," and the item was reprinted in Savannah.

episodes.title: Attempted lynching of Emma Johnson
episodes.summary: The attempted lynching of Emma Johnson took place at Summerfield, Georgia, about six miles from Macon, in March 1882, when a mob surrounded the officers holding Johnson, a young Black woman accused of killing a local merchant. The officers prevented the lynching and took her to Macon, where she was later convicted of murder in Bibb Superior Court. Papers across the country carried the story as a murder, with the mob mentioned in a single sentence.

episodes.title: Killing of Munroe Bloom
episodes.summary: The killing of Munroe Bloom was the fatal shooting of a Black man by a Georgia constable at Morrow's Station, on the Central railroad, in mid-March 1882. The constable had warrants charging Bloom and a second Black man with forgery, and Bloom, shot as he resisted arrest, was later found dead in the woods. A coroner's jury ruled the killing justifiable homicide, and the Atlanta dispatch reporting it ran in papers from Richmond and New York to Texas.

episodes.title: Assault on John H. Dorsey
episodes.summary: The assault on John H. Dorsey was an attack by a crowd on a Black man in Washington, D.C., on the afternoon of 17 March 1882. Three men named as members of the crowd were brought before the Police Court the next morning, where one was discharged and two were sentenced. The case drew only brief notices in two Washington evening papers.

episodes.title: Threatened lynching of Edward Alberson and James Eato
episodes.summary: The threatened lynching of Edward Alberson and James Eato took place at the railroad depot in Roslyn, Long Island, New York, on the night of March 25, 1882, when a crowd threatened to lynch the two Black prisoners as officers removed them to the Queens County Jail. The officers got the men onto the train, and both later stood trial in Long Island City. The threat appears in a single New-York Tribune report on a robbery case that the paper followed closely.

episodes.title: Killing of escaped convicts near Big Springs, Texas (1882)
episodes.summary: The killing of escaped convicts near Big Springs, Texas, took place in March 1882, when rangers pursuing four Black convicts who had escaped from a Texas & Pacific Railroad work gang killed two of them and captured the other two. The convicts were said to have killed a guard in the escape, and the episode ran as a brief wire item in papers from Texas to West Virginia, Utah and California.

episodes.title: Killing of Elbert Rogers
episodes.summary: The killing of Elbert Rogers was the fatal shooting of a Black man accused of horse theft in Henderson County, Texas, in March 1882. Rogers was shot in the back while being pursued by a deputy sheriff and the horse's owner and died in the jail at Athens, and a coroner's jury attributed the shot to an unknown hand.

episodes.title: Sunflower Landing smallpox shooting
episodes.summary: The Sunflower Landing smallpox shooting was an attack on an unnamed Black man ill with smallpox, who was shot and whose cabin was burned at Sunflower Landing, Mississippi, as reported in March 1882. The only known account was a single line in a Kentucky paper's news column, which did not say who carried out the attack, when it happened, or whether the man survived.

episodes.title: Burning of Floyd King's house
episodes.summary: The burning of Floyd King's house was a suspected arson in early March 1882 in which the house of Floyd King, a Black man, was burned in Oconee, apparently Oconee County, Georgia. Two white tramps were thought to be responsible, but no arrest was reported, and the burning is known only from one short paragraph in the Savannah Morning News.

episodes.title: Arkadelphia road-work shooting
episodes.summary: The Arkadelphia road-work shooting was a shooting affray in early March 1882, six miles south of Arkadelphia, Arkansas, in which two white men, Joe Ross and Bud Henry, shot three Black men, Lewis Smith, Aaron Clark and Ed Clark. Smith was killed outright and a second man was reported unable to recover, though one later roundup said all three died. The two white men escaped, and the story ran as a brief wire item from Memphis to Minnesota and Wisconsin.

episodes.title: Killing of Bill Williams (Jim Titus)
episodes.summary: The killing of Bill Williams, also reported as Jim Titus, was the fatal shooting of a Black escaped convict by Memphis police sergeant James Scott at a cabin near Overton station, Tennessee, in mid-January 1882. The officers said he attacked them with an ax when they forced the door, and they left his body where it fell. The Memphis Daily Appeal told the story at length from the officers' side, while papers in Georgia, Texas, Missouri and Mississippi carried a one-sentence wire item.

episodes.title: Expulsion of Geo. W. Randolph from Raleigh County, West Virginia
episodes.summary: The expulsion of Geo. W. Randolph was the beating and driving out of a Black schoolteacher by a mob in Raleigh County, West Virginia, reported in February 1882. According to Randolph's own statement, the mob beat him and ordered him to leave after a justice acquitted men he had had arrested, and he left to save his life. A Parkersburg paper headed its notice of the case "SHAMEFUL" while qualifying its comment on whether the statement was true.

episodes.title: Killing of James M. Davis
episodes.doubt: Beck-Tolnay lists James M. Davis (white) as lynched, Warren Co., Tenn., 1882-03-13. Our papers describe an ambush by moonshiners of a revenue officer; the month screen did not take it as a lynching. Inventory disagreement: code by our facts.
episodes.summary: The killing of James M. Davis was the ambush shooting of a deputy United States revenue collector by a concealed party of men described as moonshiners, on the Beersheba road about three miles from McMinnville, Warren County, Tennessee, on the afternoon of March 13, 1882. Davis, known as a 'celebrated raider of moonshiners,' was shot from his horse and finished with shots to the head, and the papers reported between twenty and more than thirty bullet wounds. The federal revenue service offered rewards for the killers, but no arrest appears in the coverage.

episodes.title: Rocheport disturbance of 1882
episodes.summary: The Rocheport disturbance of 1882 was a night of conflict in Rocheport, Missouri, on April 1, 1882, in which an officer fired at a Black man, Wm. Barber, and a volley from an alley later wounded several white men. No one was reported killed, about ten Black men were arrested, and seven of them were later taken to the state penitentiary. The wire carried the story across the country as a race riot, under headlines such as "Colored Rioters in Missouri" and "War of Races."

episodes.title: Lynching of Levi Harrington
episodes.summary: The lynching of Levi Harrington took place in Kansas City, Missouri, on the night of April 3, 1882, when a mob took Harrington, a young Black man, from police officers and hanged him from the Bluff street bridge. He had been arrested on suspicion after the fatal shooting of police officer Pat Jones, and newspapers soon reported that he was probably innocent. A criminal-court judge directed a grand jury to indict the lynchers for murder, and an alleged mob leader was tried in December 1882, ending in a hung jury.

episodes.title: Lynching of Joseph Smith
episodes.summary: The lynching of Joseph Smith was the hanging of Joe or Joseph Smith, a Black man, by a mob that took him from the Putnam County jail at Winfield, West Virginia, in the early hours of April 7, 1882. Smith had been jailed about a week earlier, accused of assaulting Mrs. Hill, the wife of a Chesapeake and Ohio Railway section hand, near Scott Station. Dispatches dwelt on the mob's method: sixty to seventy-five men seized a river steamer at Raymond City to reach Winfield.

episodes.title: Attempted lynching of Ed Bridges, Ben Ray and George Blakeman
episodes.summary: The attempted lynching of Ed Bridges, Ben Ray and George Blakeman took place on a Sunday night in April 1882, when an armed mob of about 150 men from Strong City surrounded the Chase County jail at Cottonwood Falls, Kansas, intending to lynch three Black prisoners. Sheriff Balch had removed the men minutes earlier, and the mob fired revolvers into the air and dispersed. The men had been charged in the fatal shooting of George Babb, a white man, and the case ended with Bridges sentenced to ten years in prison and the other two freed.

episodes.title: Shooting of Dink Batsel
episodes.summary: The shooting of Dink Batsel took place on the night of April 8, 1882, in Stringtown, a Black neighborhood of Dallas, Texas, when Police Officer Charles Clapp shot Batsel, a Black man wanted for burglary, while trying to arrest him. Clapp said he fired because he mistook a soda-water bottle in Batsel's hand for a pistol, and the wound was thought to be mortal, but Batsel escaped wounded into the brush. No report of his death was found.

episodes.title: Lynching of Henry Ivy and Sim Acoff
episodes.summary: The lynching of Henry Ivy and Sim Acoff took place in the early morning of April 13, 1882, when about forty masked men took the two Black prisoners from their guards at a school house near Brown's Station, Dallas County, Alabama. Ivy was found hanging from a tree, and Acoff's body was reported found in a swamp eleven days later, a report that was denied and then repeated. The papers presented the killing as a sequel to the murder of planter J. B. Weisinger, for which two other men had already been executed.

episodes.title: Lynching of George Hughes
episodes.summary: The lynching of George Hughes took place in northwest Kemper County, Mississippi, in April 1882, when a crowd took Hughes, a Black tenant farmer, from a constable and hanged him. Hughes had just been committed to jail by a justice of the peace on an accusation that he had raped and murdered Callie Henson, the young wife of the farmer on whose land he lived. Mississippi papers reported the accusation as proved, and several openly approved of the lynching.

episodes.title: Burning of the Clarksville smallpox cabin
episodes.summary: The burning of the Clarksville smallpox cabin took place on the night of April 17, 1882, when, by the account of Carter Russell, a Black smallpox patient, and his nurse, unknown parties ordered them out of his quarantine cabin outside Clarksville, Tennessee, on pain of death and burned it. The Clarksville Weekly Chronicle reported that many residents believed the two had set the fire themselves, yet called the burning a "disgraceful act." Russell was later moved to tents under armed guard and died of smallpox there on April 26.

episodes.title: Stoning of Black railroad workmen at Lynchburg
episodes.summary: The stoning of Black railroad workmen at Lynchburg was an attack in 1882, some time before April 4, in which a party of young men threw stones at "the colored workmen" on the Richmond and Alleghany railroad at Lynchburg, Virginia. Several of the attackers were fined by the Mayor, while a Black worker who broke one attacker's collar-bone was sent on to the grand jury.

episodes.title: Yorkville whipping-party shooting
episodes.summary: The Yorkville whipping-party shooting was the accidental killing of Alex. Terrell near Yorkville, Gibson County, Tennessee, on a Sunday night in early April 1882, when, according to one report, a group of "boys" had gone out to whip a Black man. Terrell was shot in the neck and killed by Charles King, and no whipping is reported to have been carried out. Three Tennessee papers noted the death, but only the Rugbeian mentioned the whipping errand.

episodes.title: Killing of Erasmus Coffman
episodes.summary: The killing of Erasmus Coffman was the fatal shooting of a Black convict laborer by a guard on a Valley Railroad construction contract near Staunton, Virginia, about 19 April 1882. According to the Staunton papers, Coffman was shot while attempting to escape and was killed. The shooting was reported in brief local items and in one Washington news column.

episodes.title: Threatened lynching of Frank Johnson and Enoch Echols
episodes.summary: The threatened lynching of Frank Johnson and Enoch Echols was an attempt in April 1882 by armed white men from counties around Athens, Georgia, to take two young Black prisoners from the Athens jail and lynch them for the shooting of a University student, Walter Rountree. According to the Athens Banner, an advance guard of about 150 men was met outside town by a committee of citizens and went home without reaching the jail. The two men were later convicted of assault with intent to murder after a post-mortem traced the fatal bullet to the pistol of Rountree's own brother.

episodes.title: Terrell gambling raid shooting
episodes.summary: The Terrell gambling raid shooting took place on the night of April 27, 1882, when the city marshal of Terrell, Texas, fired three pistol shots at a man fleeing a raid on a "colored gambling den." The man escaped unhurt, and one arrest was made in the raid.

episodes.title: Threatened lynching of Houston Whiting
episodes.doubt: lynching threats during a manhunt; arrested without incident
episodes.summary: The threatened lynching of Houston Whiting took place in Charleston, West Virginia, in early May 1882, after Whiting, a Black barber, was accused of shooting a white man, T. S. Greaver, outside a saloon. While officers searched for him, papers reported threats to lynch him once caught, but he was arrested the next afternoon and no attack on him was reported.

episodes.title: Shooting of Richard Williams
episodes.summary: The shooting of Richard Williams took place in Kansas City on May 1, 1882, when Warren Landers, a clerk in a shoe house, shot Williams, a Black porter. The quarrel was said to have begun when Landers walked through a pile of dirt the porter had swept up, and Landers fled to Kentucky afterward. The shooting reached readers outside Missouri only as a brief wire item that did not report Williams's condition.

episodes.title: Mock hanging of Ned at Sherman, Wyoming
episodes.summary: The mock hanging of Ned at Sherman, Wyoming, took place on 3 May 1882, when Sherman men hoisted a Black chore boy called Ned by a rope over a cigar theft. After a barn burned, pursuers caught him again; the Cheyenne Daily Leader reported a second use of the rope, which a Sherman resident denied.

episodes.title: Masked men's seizure of the Davis murder pistol
episodes.summary: The masked men's seizure of the Davis murder pistol was an episode in Tennessee in May 1882 in which eight masked men went at night to the cabin of a Black woman and, with threats, demanded a pistol she had found near the scene of a recent murder. Told that her landlord, Mr. Phelps, had it, they called him to his window and took it from him; no one was reported hurt. The McMinnville New Era, whose item was reprinted in Winchester, treated the episode as a likely sign that the band knew something about the killing of Capt. James M. Davis.

episodes.title: Lynching of Sam Shelton and Jim Keys
episodes.summary: The lynching of Sam Shelton and Jim Keys took place at Belton, Bell County, Texas, about 1 a.m. on the night of Saturday, May 20, 1882, when a mob of masked men took the two prisoners, one white and one Black, from the county jail and hanged them to a tree. No one in the mob was identified, and an inquest was reported to have found the men died at the hands of parties unknown. Texas papers treated it as a return of the mob rule that had long troubled Bell County.

episodes.title: Hardeeville bridge hands shooting
episodes.summary: The Hardeeville bridge hands shooting was the killing of a Black laborer by a white mechanic from Baltimore at the railroad station in Hardeeville, South Carolina, on the night of Saturday, May 27, 1882. The shooting was reported as self-defense, and the papers gave most attention to what followed, when Black workers tried to seize the white men and, in the wire's words, "attempted to lynch the killer, but were prevented."

episodes.title: Killing of Wilson Edwards
episodes.summary: The killing of Wilson Edwards was the fatal shooting of a Black prisoner by a member of a sheriff's posse in the jail at Monroe, North Carolina, in late May 1882. Edwards, held on a peace warrant, was shot as Sheriff A. J. Price and a group of helpers tried to put him in irons, and a coroner's jury found the shooting justifiable. North Carolina papers printed detailed accounts from the officers' side, and a short wire item carried the story to Tennessee, Alabama and Missouri as the death of 'a notorious desperado'.

episodes.title: Pursuit of Jim Williams near Plano
episodes.doubt: pursuers vowed Judge Lynch; no capture reported
episodes.summary: The pursuit of Jim Williams near Plano was a manhunt in Collin County, Texas, on May 31, 1882, in which ten or twelve armed citizens chased a farm hand accused of attempted rape and said they would lynch him if they caught him. The only account, a Plano dispatch to the Dallas Herald, left him at large, and no report of his capture or death was found.

episodes.title: Mock hanging of Dave Jackson in the Fort Worth jail
episodes.summary: The mock hanging of Dave Jackson took place in the county jail at Fort Worth, Texas, in the spring of 1882, when prisoners held a "kangaroo court," found Jackson, a Black prisoner, guilty, and strung him up to a rafter. He was nearly dead when he was cut down. A brief about the episode ran in newspapers across the South and in Ohio as a macabre curiosity.

episodes.title: Hanging-torture of Zachariah Johnson
episodes.summary: The hanging-torture of Zachariah Johnson was an assault in May 1882 or shortly before, in which a mob in Union County, reported as in Indiana by most papers and in Arkansas by one, repeatedly hanged a Black man to force him to confess to a theft. Johnson survived, and the county sheriff and one or two deputies were reported arrested as participants. The story circulated as a short item in papers in North Carolina, Vermont and Pennsylvania.

episodes.title: Assault on Cole near Dardanelle
episodes.summary: The assault on Cole near Dardanelle was an attack on a Black man named Cole by a crowd of armed and masked men near Dardanelle, Arkansas, on a Wednesday night in May 1882, probably 17 May. Cole was badly cut about the face and head, pulled the mask from one attacker he said he recognized, and took out warrants against the men.

episodes.title: Brighton train attack on Joliet strikebreakers
episodes.summary: The Brighton train attack was an assault by about fifty striking iron workers on non-union laborers of the Joliet Iron and Steel Company aboard a Chicago & Alton train at Brighton, Chicago, on the evening of June 1, 1882. Most of those dragged out and beaten were Black workers, and a stray shot wounded Judge N. J. Pillsbury of the Illinois appellate court, a passenger. No one was reported killed, several men were arrested, and the story ran nationally within coverage of the iron strike.

episodes.title: Lynching of Caleb Campbell
episodes.summary: The lynching of Caleb Campbell took place on the night of June 2, 1882, when about eighty disguised riders took Campbell, a Black man, from the jail at Winnsboro, South Carolina, and hanged him from a tree three miles outside town. Campbell was being held for trial on a charge of attempting to assault a white woman near Blythewood in Fairfield County. A coroner's jury found that he had been murdered by persons unknown, and the Winnsboro newspaper published an editorial defending the lynching.

episodes.title: Epes fire and expulsion of 1882
episodes.summary: The Epes fire and expulsion of 1882 was a clash in Epes, Sumter County, Alabama, on June 3, 1882, in which white men drove a crowd of Black men out of town and the town was burned that night. Seven stores burned, four Black men accused of setting the fire were arrested at Tuscaloosa, and papers reported fears that they would be lynched. The story ran widely in the white press as a case of "negro incendiaries" and "negro rioters."

episodes.title: Lynching of three men at Butlerville, Arkansas
episodes.summary: The lynching of three men at Butlerville, Arkansas, took place on the night of Sunday, June 4, 1882, when a mob took three Black men from officers at Butlerville, in Lonoke County, and hanged them to a tree. The men, who were not named, were accused of assaulting a thirteen-year-old girl, Annie Bridges, although an earlier report had called the story untrue. A Little Rock dispatch of June 5 carried the news to papers across the country, many under headlines presenting the hanging as just punishment.

episodes.title: Lewisville cabin shooting and rapes (1882)
episodes.summary: The Lewisville cabin shooting and rapes took place on the night of June 4, 1882, near Lewisville, Texas, when a group of armed men shot into the cabin of Perry Bolin, a Black man, forced their way in and raped two Black women. The accusation surfaced at a hearing on a separate complaint by two farmers whom the same men had shot at that night, and officers were reported to be pursuing the three accused.

episodes.title: Burning of Thomas J. Archer's farm, Cardington, Ohio
episodes.summary: The burning of Thomas J. Archer's farm took place near Cardington, Ohio, on the night of June 5, 1882, when a mob burned the house, barn and farm buildings of Archer, a Black man, while he was held in jail for shooting three people. The sheriff kept Archer from a crowd that had threatened to lynch him, and the story circulated in Ohio and beyond because the quarrel was said to have begun with neighbors refusing to call him "Mister Archer."

episodes.title: Lynching of George Beckett
episodes.summary: The lynching of George Beckett took place at Aberdeen, Monroe County, Mississippi, early on the morning of June 2, 1882, when a crowd took Beckett, a Black man, from the county jail and hanged him. He had been accused of attempting to outrage a girl of about seven years old. The case reached papers across the country ten days later through a St. Louis Post-Dispatch wire that misdated it to June 11, and was paired in news digests with lynchings at Rock Hill, South Carolina, and Lawrence, Kansas.

episodes.title: Attempted lynching of Alex Murray and Charles Shelby
episodes.summary: The attempted lynching of Alex Murray and Charles Shelby took place at the Livingston County jail in Chillicothe, Missouri, about 1 a.m. on the night of June 11-12, 1882, when a crowd of men demanded two young Black prisoners accused of shooting a telegraph operator. Sheriff Leeper refused to give them up and threatened to shoot, and the crowd scattered after shots were fired, with no one hurt.

episodes.title: Lynching of John Johnson
episodes.summary: The lynching of John Johnson was the hanging of a 17-year-old Black youth by a crowd at Rock Hill, South Carolina, early on the morning of June 12, 1882. Johnson had been accused of assaulting Alice McDowell, a white girl, the day before, and was taken from a guard and hanged from a tree on Main Street. A coroner's jury found that he was hanged by persons unknown, and a Charleston wire carried the news to papers across the country.

episodes.title: Lynching of Jim Mitchell
episodes.summary: The lynching of Jim Mitchell took place on the night of June 14, 1882, at Mount Sterling, Kentucky, where armed men took Mitchell, a Black man, from the jail and hanged him from a railroad trestle. Mitchell had been jailed that day, accused of assaulting the wife of a local farmer. The Louisville dispatch that carried the story across the country said the whole community approved of the lynching.

episodes.title: Lynching of Thomas Wall and Trinidad Charlie
episodes.summary: The lynching of Thomas Wall and Trinidad Charlie took place at Rico, Colorado, at about 2 a.m. on June 16, 1882, when a party entered the town jail, took out the two prisoners and hanged them in a small cabin opposite. The men were accused of killing Rico's marshal, and the wire report of their deaths ran in papers across the country under headings such as "Two Murderers Lynched in Colorado." Only one syndicated brief described them as "two colored desperadoes."

episodes.title: Lynching of Henry Huddleston
episodes.summary: The lynching of Henry Huddleston took place in Winchester, Franklin County, Tennessee, on the night of Sunday, June 18, 1882, when a crowd of men seized Huddleston, a young Black man, from guards in a room of the courthouse and hanged him from a tree in the courthouse yard. He had been accused of raping Mrs. Matt Vaughan, a white widow of the town, the night before. A coroner's jury found that he died by hanging "by the hands of unknown parties," and the story ran as a brief wire item in papers from Virginia to Utah.

episodes.title: Lynching of Morgan Hamilton
episodes.summary: The lynching of Morgan Hamilton was the shooting of a Black farm worker by a party of men carrying an arrest warrant in a field near Booneville, Mississippi, on the morning of Saturday, June 17, 1882. Hamilton had been accused of the murder of Miss Serena Benton and released by the inquest jury; the eight or ten men who went to re-arrest him shot him as he ran, and the sheriff set out after them. A Mississippi correspondent called the killing an outrage committed "on mere suspicion," while wire copy carried it across the country as the shooting of an accused murderer.

episodes.title: Killing of Griffin Ingram
episodes.summary: The killing of Griffin Ingram was the shooting of a Black man by a member of a constable's posse on the Ponchatolowa in St. Tammany Parish, Louisiana, on June 21, 1882. Ingram was wanted on a warrant from Livingston parish, accused of murdering his young son, and the local paper reported that he was shot while resisting arrest. An inquest was held on his body, and the parish later paid its costs.

episodes.title: Lynching of Milan Howard
episodes.summary: The lynching of Milan Howard took place at the bridge over Bonfouca, in St. Tammany Parish, Louisiana, in June 1882, when about sixty men took Howard, a Black man accused of rape, from a constable and hanged him from the bridge. The parish paper approved the killing, and the parish later paid for his burial as a man "hung by unknown parties." Outside Louisiana the hanging circulated mainly as a joke item claiming that Oscar Wilde had watched it from a train.

episodes.title: Stabbing of Bernard McNally during the Baltimore G.A.R. parade
episodes.summary: The McNally stabbing in Baltimore took place on the evening of 21 June 1882, when boys threw stones at a parading Black division of the Grand Army of the Republic and a member of the column fatally stabbed Bernard McNally, a youth standing at the corner of Madison and Constitution streets. George H. Brightman, the Black vice-commander of Lincoln Post, was charged with murder after a coroner's jury named him, but he was acquitted in December 1882 when the state conceded its evidence was insufficient.

episodes.title: Elm Bottom lynching report (1882)
episodes.doubt: Dallas Herald called the report a hoax; race of the dead never given
episodes.summary: The Elm Bottom lynching report of 1882 was a widely circulated account that the bodies of four men, two hanged and two shot, had been found in the Elm bottom of Denton County, Texas, on the morning of June 22, 1882. Wire dispatches from Dallas presented the deaths as a lynching of cowboys or cattle thieves, and the story ran in papers from California to New Hampshire. The Dallas Daily Herald, the nearest paper in the coverage, doubted the rumor from the start and the next day called it a hoax.

episodes.title: Lynching of John Tolly
episodes.summary: The lynching of John Tolly was the hanging of a young Black man by a mob at Elizabethtown, Illinois, on the evening of Monday, June 26, 1882. He was accused of trying to break into the house of Mrs. Howe, but she could not identify him, and a witness said he had been elsewhere. Papers across the country carried the story because the man hanged was believed to be innocent, under headlines such as "Hanged the Wrong Man."

episodes.title: Sale of John Hanson
episodes.summary: The sale of John Hanson was the public auction of a Black man into a year's servitude at the courthouse door in Louisville, Kentucky, on June 14, 1882, as punishment for vagrancy. A city scavenger bought him for two dollars. Papers across the country reported it as a return of slavery, the first such sale in the city since before the Civil War.

episodes.title: Third Ward polling-place assaults, Wilmington, 1882
episodes.summary: The Third Ward polling-place assaults took place on 3 June 1882 at the Third Ward polls in Wilmington, Delaware, during a municipal election, when a crowd of Democrats drove colored voters from the polls and beat two men who vouched for them. Mr. Burchall was badly beaten and Edmund Mitchell nearly killed, according to the Republican Daily Republican, the only paper found to report the assaults.

episodes.title: Lynching of George Washington (New Mexico, 1882)
episodes.summary: The lynching of George Washington was the hanging by a mob of a Black man from Lincoln, New Mexico Territory, reported in June 1882. The only account found connects his death to his having eloped with a Mexican girl, and gives no date, place or names of the mob.

episodes.title: Racquet Club arrests
episodes.summary: The Racquet Club arrests took place in New York on the night of June 8, 1882, when a policeman entered the Racquet Club on Sixth Avenue to arrest John Whitehurst, a Black waiter accused of taking a purse, without a warrant. After two of the men he was serving objected, police reinforcements took the waiter and the club men to the station house, and Whitehurst later testified that the arresting officer struck him twice. The papers treated it mainly as a dispute over the club men's rights, and in July a police justice ruled the arrest lawful.

episodes.title: Houston Emancipation Day shooting
episodes.summary: The Houston Emancipation Day shooting took place before daylight on June 20, 1882, at the grounds where Black residents of Houston, Texas, were celebrating emancipation. Charles F. Witham, a white printer, was shot dead, Deputy Marshal Wm. Glass was wounded, and a Black man was killed and two Black people wounded by what the dispatches called stray shots. Several Black men were arrested, and three were later charged with Witham's murder.

episodes.title: Duval County polygamist shooting
episodes.summary: The Duval County polygamist shooting was the shooting of an unnamed Black man in Duval County, Florida, by a man described as a polygamist with three wives, reported in April 1882. The victim had been on his way to the court-house to file a complaint against the polygamist when he was overtaken and shot. The story survives only as a brief paragraph credited to the Chicago News that newspapers across the country reprinted as a curiosity.

episodes.title: Shooting of Canless Blair
episodes.summary: The shooting of Canless Blair took place in or near Shelby, Cleveland County, North Carolina, in May 1882, when a sheriff's officer, B. F. Logan, wounded Blair, a Black man said to be an escaped convict, with rifle fire. A pistol shot that Blair was said to have fired at the officers struck George Wright, another Black man, in the leg. Blair survived and was jailed; the two papers that reported it told the officers' version.

episodes.title: Killing of Monroe by a Clayton County bailiff
episodes.summary: The killing of Monroe was the shooting of a Black man named Monroe by a bailiff in Clayton County, Georgia, on March 15, 1882, while the bailiff tried to arrest him and another Black man, John Brown, on a charge of theft or forgery. Brown escaped and was captured weeks later at a railroad job in Monroe County, and the episode reached print mainly as a story about his arrest.

episodes.title: Lynching of Frank Fisher
episodes.summary: The lynching of Frank Fisher took place on Sunday afternoon, April 30, 1882, at Galion, Crawford County, Ohio, when a crowd broke into the City Hall prison, took out Fisher, a Black man accused of raping a thirteen-year-old girl, and hanged him in nearby woods. He protested his innocence to the end. Ohio papers remarked that it was done by unmasked men, in daylight, on a Sunday, before thousands of onlookers.

episodes.title: Attempted lynching of the Gordon brothers at Vincennes, Indiana
episodes.summary: The attempted lynching of the Gordon brothers was a failed attempt by a mob at Vincennes, Indiana, to take two Black brothers named Gordon out of jail and hang them some time between October 1881 and April 1882. The brothers, accused of robbing an elderly couple, were saved by the sheriff and later convicted, after which a third brother declared that he and an uncle had committed the crime.

episodes.title: Lynching of Peter Vinegar, George Robertson and Isaac King
episodes.summary: The lynching of Peter Vinegar, George Robertson and Isaac King took place at Lawrence, Kansas, early on June 10, 1882, when masked men took the three Black prisoners from the Douglas County jail and hanged them from the Kansas river bridge. The men were charged with robbing and killing David Bausman, an Ohio farmer, and were reported to have confessed at a preliminary examination the day before. The case drew national wire coverage, a protest meeting by Black residents, and condemnation from Kansas papers.

episodes.title: Lynching of Jim Sanders
episodes.summary: The lynching of Jim Sanders was the shooting of a Black youth of about 18 by masked men in Union township, Arkansas, about ten to twelve miles from Little Rock, on the night of May 28, 1882. Sanders had been arrested that afternoon on an accusation of attempting to assault a white girl and was held under a constable's guard when the band broke in and killed him. The killing angered Black residents of the area, and Little Rock papers reported fears of a clash between white and Black residents in the following week.

episodes.title: Lynching of Joseph E. Jenkins and Eugene Azar
episodes.summary: The lynching of Joseph E. Jenkins and Eugene Azar took place on May 15, 1882, when a crowd of about 200 to 300 men took Jenkins, a white man held on a murder charge, from the parish jail at St. Martinsville, Louisiana, and hanged him near Breaux Bridge, together with Azar, a Black man seized on the way. Governor S. D. McEnery offered a $2,000 reward, and sixteen men were later jailed, but a St. Martin Parish grand jury returned no true bill and the prisoners were released. Papers across the country noted that the second victim, out on bond on a lesser or disputed charge, had simply been met on the road, and later dispatches reported armed Black residents swearing vengeance.

episodes.title: Lynching of Nathan Laird
episodes.summary: The lynching of Nathan Laird was the hanging of a Black prisoner by a masked mob that took him from the jail at Sardis, Mississippi, early on the morning of June 21, 1882. Laird, named 'Nathan Lucid' in the wire report and 'Frank Layard' in a Memphis paper, was awaiting trial on a charge of raping or assaulting members of a white widow's household. The Sardis paper gave a detailed account of the jail raid, while papers across the country carried a one-sentence wire item.

episodes.title: Lynching of William Smeal
episodes.summary: The lynching of William Smeal was the hanging of a Black farm worker by a group of men near the Jefferson and Lawrenceville road in Gwinnett County, Georgia, in mid-February 1882. Suspected of stealing a horse, Smeal was taken from his cabin at night, whipped until he confessed, and hanged with a trace chain to a tree. An Athens wire dispatch carried the story to papers across the country, and a local weekly condemned the killing as "lynch law."

episodes.title: Lynching of Ed Sayles
episodes.summary: The lynching of Ed Sayles was the hanging of a Black youth by a masked band at Iredell, Texas, on the night of July 6, 1882. Sayles, accused that morning of raping a farmer's wife, was taken from his guards and hanged from a pecan tree near the depot. The wire carried the story across the country, often under headlines that approved the killing.

episodes.title: Lynching of Mack Taylor
episodes.summary: The lynching of Mack Taylor was the killing of a 14-year-old Black boy in Webster Parish, Louisiana, in June 1882 by three white men who seized him in Arkansas, brought him back, tied him to a tree and shot him. A coroner's jury named Edward McDonald, the father of a white boy Taylor was accused of beating, and two men who helped him. A Shreveport dispatch describing the remains as picked bare by vultures ran in papers across the country under headlines of revenge and butchery.

episodes.title: Lynching of William Ritter
episodes.summary: The lynching of William Ritter took place in the early hours of July 12, 1882, when a masked mob took Ritter, a Black man, from the jail at Henderson, Kentucky, and hanged him on a tree about a mile outside the town. Ritter had been charged with the rape and murder of Helen Brewster, a Black girl from the county. The papers treated the case as notable because the mob was reported to include both Black and white men, and the Henderson Reporter called it the first lynching in the county's history.

episodes.title: Rock Creek assault on Eunice Martin
episodes.doubt: police partly deny the assault by three youths
episodes.summary: The Rock Creek assault on Eunice Martin was a reported attack on an eight-year-old Black girl by three white youths near the Twentieth street bridge over Rock Creek in Washington, D.C., in mid-July 1882. The Evening Critic and an Associated Press dispatch described it as a sexual assault that left the child in critical condition, but a police report days later said she had only been driven from a spring and stoned. Several boys were arrested and all were discharged.

episodes.title: Killing of a smallpox patient near Red Clay, Georgia
episodes.summary: The killing of a smallpox patient near Red Clay, Georgia, took place in mid-July 1882, when railroad laborers shot an unnamed Black man who had been quarantined in an isolated cabin and then set the cabin on fire. Warrants were issued against several men, but the local paper reported no conclusive evidence of who took part. A one-line wire item carried the killing across the country, and a fuller Georgia account was later reprinted as 'Murder as a Cure for Small-Pox.'

episodes.title: Lynching of Dennis McLellan
episodes.summary: The lynching of Dennis McLellan took place in Kemper County, Mississippi, on July 15, 1882, when armed men took the Black youth from a deputy's guard on the road to the county jail at DeKalb and, it was supposed, hanged him. He had been accused of entering the bedroom of a Kemper County man's ten-year-old daughter the night before. The only source, the Meridian Observer, did not confirm his death but endorsed the lynching, and papers that reprinted it praised the act.

episodes.title: Lynching of David Cook
episodes.summary: The lynching of David Cook was the killing of a young Black man by masked men in northern Kershaw County, South Carolina, in July 1882, after he was taken from officers who were conveying him to Camden. Cook, accused of attempted rape, was seized on Saturday, July 15, and his body was found two days later hanging from a tree. A Charleston wire report carried the story to papers across the country, most of them repeating its claim that he had confessed.

episodes.title: Rockmart tunnel riot
episodes.summary: The Rockmart tunnel riot was a gunfight on July 15, 1882, at a railroad tunnel in Paulding County, Georgia, about seven miles from Rockmart, after a white man, John Hicks, tried without authority to disarm Black railroad hands. Hicks's party shot a Black worker named Tom Laws, who was reported dying and later dead, and the Black workers then killed Hicks. The papers treated it as a race riot, and it ended in the arrest of some thirty Black workers, four life sentences for murder and a death sentence for a man called the riot's leader.

episodes.title: Musick's Ferry mob attack on Franz Suppenbach
episodes.summary: The Musick's Ferry mob attack on Franz Suppenbach took place in mid-July 1882 at Musick's Ferry, St. Louis County, Missouri, when a crowd of Black men went at night to the house of a German laborer who was living with a Black woman. The German fired a musket into the crowd, and first wire reports said he had killed a preacher and was then drowned or hanged by the mob. Corrections a week later said that no one had died and that the man, named in them as Franz Suppenbach, had walked to St. Louis with the woman.

episodes.title: Killing of George Bentley
episodes.summary: The killing of George Bentley was the fatal shooting of a Black miner from Marietta, Georgia, by a white man named Sam Hunt at the copper mines in Haralson County, Georgia, in early July 1882. Hunt fled after the shooting, and two other miners were jailed over an earlier roadside assault. An Atlanta wire report presented Hunt as a constable who killed a miner resisting arrest, while Bentley's hometown paper described him only as a white man who returned with friends after losing a fight.

episodes.title: Attempted lynching of Noah Parks
episodes.summary: The attempted lynching of Noah Parks was the hanging of a Black preacher by a mob in Winston County, Mississippi, in the summer of 1882. Accused of stealing corn, Parks was taken from his house at night and hanged to a tree, but friends cut him down and revived him. The story ran nationally as a brief wire item, and at least one Western paper treated it as a completed lynching and endorsed it.

episodes.title: Attempted lynching of Alfred Ross
episodes.summary: The attempted lynching of Alfred Ross took place in Memphis, Tennessee, on the evening of July 24, 1882, when a crowd tried to hang Ross, a Black steamboat roustabout, as officers brought him out to be identified. Ross had been accused that morning of striking an aged Italian grocer, John Genochio, with a rock. Bystanders held the crowd back, and Ross was later bound over to the Criminal Court.

episodes.title: Castration of Eli McKnight
episodes.summary: The castration of Eli McKnight was a mob attack on a Black man near Gurdon station, Arkansas, on the night of Tuesday, July 25, 1882. Accused of trying to rape Miss Baker, a young woman of the neighborhood, he was captured that evening and castrated by a mob, and a Little Rock Gazette dispatch reported that he would recover. The story spread by wire to papers from Tennessee to Pennsylvania and Washington, D.C., often under headlines that treated the mutilation as a deserved punishment.

episodes.title: Lynching of Martin Becket
episodes.summary: The lynching of Martin Becket was the killing of a Black man taken from the jail at Hampton Courthouse, South Carolina, on the night of Tuesday, July 25, 1882. Becket had been jailed on an accusation of assaulting a white girl about twelve years old, and a crowd reported at some three hundred took him out and lynched him. A placard reading "Our women must be protected" was left with his body, and its words became the headline under which the story ran across the country.

episodes.title: Threatened lynching of Otho Gilmore
episodes.summary: The threatened lynching of Otho Gilmore took place at Martin's Ferry, Belmont County, Ohio, on the night of July 26, 1882, when a large crowd talked of hanging Gilmore, a Black prisoner, after he cut a police officer and a citizen with a razor in the town lockup. A guard was placed at the jail, and the crowd broke up once the wounded men were expected to live. Gilmore, who had been shot twice by the officer, recovered and was sentenced in December to four years in the penitentiary.

episodes.title: Lynching of Henry Caldwell
episodes.summary: The lynching of Henry Caldwell took place shortly after midnight on July 30, 1882, when a disguised mob took Caldwell, a Black man held on a charge of assaulting an elderly white woman, from the Iron County jail at Ironton, Missouri, and hanged and shot him from the Iron Mountain Railroad bridge. A coroner's jury found that he died at the hands of a mob whose members were unknown to it. The local weekly endorsed the killing, while St. Louis wire reports carried it to papers across the country under headlines such as 'A Ravisher Lynched.'

episodes.title: Killing of Frank Clinton
episodes.summary: The killing of Frank Clinton was the shooting of a Black man at Marion, Mississippi, by unknown parties, reported in July 1882. Clinton, who was said to have had two children with a white woman, was "riddled with forty-eight bullets," and the only report found gives no motive, names no attackers and records no arrests.

episodes.title: Brooksville courthouse shooting
episodes.summary: The Brooksville courthouse shooting was a clash at the Hernando County courthouse in Brooksville, Florida, on the afternoon of June 29, 1882, in which white townspeople shot and killed three Black brothers, Henry, Jim and Rube Turner. Several other Black men were wounded and two or more white men were slightly hurt. Carried nationally from Jacksonville under headlines such as "Conflict of Races" and "A War of Races," the story was told entirely from the white side and blamed the Turners for the fight.

episodes.title: Killing of Primus Johnson
episodes.summary: The killing of Primus Johnson was the death of a Black man at Shell Mound, on the Tallahatchie River in Mississippi, in early August 1882, during a white posse's pursuit of a Black man accused of attacking a white planter. A telegraphic report said the posse captured Johnson and a mob shot him dead, while a Mississippi paper said he was killed trying to escape from officers.

episodes.title: Police killing of Frank Hagan
episodes.summary: The police killing of Frank Hagan took place near Leavenworth, Kansas, in early August 1882, when a policeman shot Hagan, a Black man, three times while trying to arrest him after a shooting at an emancipation celebration. Hagan died on August 4, and a coroner's inquest exculpated the officer, identified in a follow-up dispatch as Policeman Shepherd. The story ran as a short telegraphic item in papers from Memphis to Savannah, one of which headed it "A Negro Desperado Killed."

episodes.title: Killing of Sandy Bynum
episodes.summary: The killing of Sandy Bynum was the fatal shooting of a Black Republican leader by Thomas G. Hewlett, a former U.S. deputy marshal, at a political barbecue at Ayer's Spring near Huntsville, Alabama, on August 5, 1882. Hewlett fled on horseback, was later tried for second-degree murder, and was acquitted. Telegraphed across the country, the killing became a talking point in the partisan press over political violence in the South.

episodes.title: Attempted lynching of William Holmes
episodes.summary: The attempted lynching of William Holmes took place on the night of Sunday, August 6, 1882, when a mob of about a hundred men surrounded the jail at Pomeroy, Ohio, to seize Holmes, a Black man charged with outraging a young white girl near Rutland. The men nearly broke through the jail walls before learning that Holmes had already been taken away and sent to Columbus for safekeeping. The case drew further notice when two alleged leaders of the mob, both of Middleport, were arrested and jailed, and their friends threatened to free them by force.

episodes.title: Eastman camp meeting riot
episodes.summary: The Eastman camp meeting riot took place on Sunday, August 6, 1882, at Eastman, Dodge County, Georgia, when the town marshal's party shot dead a Black prisoner fleeing arrest and a crowd of Black excursionists then killed a young white man, James Q. Harvard, whom they took for one of the officers. Two accounts add that armed white citizens then killed three Black men in a clash with the crowd. Twenty-two Black defendants were convicted of Harvard's murder, five were hanged together at Eastman in October, and the two officers were indicted for manslaughter.

episodes.title: Lynching of Dan Blakeney
episodes.summary: The lynching of Dan Blakeney was the hanging of a Black farm hand near Lancaster, South Carolina, on August 8, 1882, by a body of men who took him from constables escorting him to jail. He had been accused of attempting to assault the twelve-year-old daughter of his employer the night before. The Charleston News and Courier's Lancaster correspondent, who saw the body, endorsed the killing, and a short wire version of his report ran in papers across the country.

episodes.title: Lynching of A. Brown (Sam Miller)
episodes.summary: The lynching of A. Brown (Sam Miller) was the hanging of a Black man by a party of men who took him from the jail at Newnan, Georgia, on the night of August 9, 1882. He had been accused of outraging a fifteen-year-old white girl in Campbell County and brought to Newnan for safe keeping. An Atlanta dispatch carried the story across the country within a day, and several papers printed it under headings approving the killing.

episodes.title: Lynching of John Mullins
episodes.summary: The lynching of John Mullins was the shooting of a Black man by a crowd of about fifteen men at his sister's house on Topisaw, near Tyler's mill, Mississippi, on the night of August 10, 1882. Mullins had been accused of attempting an outrage on a white woman in Lawrence County, and the local paper reported his killing under the heading "The Perpetrator Summarily Dealt with."

episodes.title: Killing of Booth near Satartia
episodes.summary: The killing of Booth was the fatal shooting of a Black man named Booth near Satartia, Yazoo County, Mississippi, on Saturday, August 12, 1882, by two white men after he refused to let them ride in his wagon. Both men escaped, and a Jackson dispatch on the shooting ran in papers across the country, several of which headlined it as murder.

episodes.title: Lynching of Bob Young and Charlie Griffin
episodes.summary: The lynching of Bob Young and Charlie Griffin was the hanging of two Black prisoners by a mob of about forty men near La Fayette, Chambers County, Alabama, in August 1882. The two had been convicted of murdering a white man named McCann, but their conviction had been reversed on appeal and a new trial ordered when the mob took them from the jail. Wire reports carried the killing to papers across the country, several of which noted that the men protested their innocence to the end.

episodes.title: Cowtown attack on the Washington poundmen
episodes.summary: The Cowtown attack on the Washington poundmen was an assault by a crowd of residents of the 'Cowtown' neighborhood of Washington, D.C., on the city poundmaster and his men on the morning of August 19, 1882, in which a Black poundman, Albert Fortune, was struck on the head with a stone. During the fray a resident, John Keefe, called for a gun to 'kill the niggers', and four residents were fined or forfeited collateral in Police Court.

episodes.title: Lynching of Jack Turner
episodes.summary: The lynching of Jack Turner took place at Butler, the county seat of Choctaw County, Alabama, on August 19, 1882, when a crowd took Turner, a Black Republican leader, from jail and hanged him on the vote of a mass meeting. He had been jailed with several other Black men on the charge of leading a plot to massacre the county's white population, a charge resting on papers said to have been found by two white men. Republican papers and Black Republicans called the plot an invention meant to intimidate Black voters, and the governor's office asked county officers for an investigation, which they answered with a defense of the hanging.

episodes.title: Attempted lynching of Liberty Kennedy
episodes.summary: The attempted lynching of Liberty Kennedy took place in Hannibal, Missouri, on August 22, 1882, when a crowd of white citizens chased down Kennedy, a young Black man accused with Edward Murphy of assaulting a white girl, and relatives of the girl tried to kill him. The attempt failed and both men were jailed, but the wire dispatch that carried the story across the country predicted they would be lynched at their examination.

episodes.title: Killing of Ben Harris
episodes.summary: The killing of Ben Harris took place on August 26, 1882, near Visalia, Tulare County, California, when a Black man accused of murdering his stepdaughter and wounding his wife was shot dead by a pursuer, John Dice, while trying to escape. Harris had been hunted for four days by a party of twenty or thirty men, and wire reports of both the killings and his death ran in papers across the country.

episodes.title: Lynching of Smith near Little Rock
episodes.summary: The lynching of Smith near Little Rock was the killing of a Black man known only as Smith by a disguised party in Arkansas on or about August 24, 1882. He was accused of attempting to outrage a white woman, and a wire dispatch reporting that he had been shot to death ran in papers across the country within days.

episodes.title: Lynching of Leonard Coker
episodes.summary: The lynching of Leonard Coker was the hanging of a Black man by a crowd of whites and blacks near Cowles Station, Alabama, about 30 miles east of Montgomery, on August 25, 1882. Coker was accused of outraging and murdering a white woman, most often named as Catharine Haynes, and was hanged to a tree at the scene of the alleged crime after a search and a reported confession. An Associated Press dispatch from Montgomery carried the story to papers across the country, several of which presented the killing as deserved.

episodes.title: Lynching of Charles Savage and Howard James
episodes.summary: The lynching of Charles Savage and Howard James was the shooting of two Black prisoners by a mob at the railroad depot in Madison, Florida, on the morning of August 25, 1882. The men, convicted of the 1881 killing of Frank Patterson but granted a new trial, were being taken under a sheriff's guard to Jasper for retrial when armed men stopped the train and shot them. Governor William D. Bloxham offered a $5,000 reward, but a coroner's jury found that they died at the hands of parties unknown, and no one was reported tried.

episodes.title: Nettleton railroad laborers' expulsion
episodes.summary: The Nettleton railroad laborers' expulsion was the driving off of Black construction workers from a railroad line near Nettleton, Craighead County, Arkansas, in mid-August 1882 by armed men disguised as Ku Klux. The contractors and the railroad's president appealed to Governor T. J. Churchill, who ordered the county sheriff to protect the workers, and within a week the men were reported back at work. Papers across the country carried the story as a revival of the Ku Klux and a clash between white and Black laborers.

episodes.title: Prineville lynching rumor of August 1882
episodes.doubt: rumor that five boys were lynched; dossier finds it contested
episodes.summary: The Prineville lynching rumor of August 1882 was a report, carried to Albany, Oregon, by a traveler, that a mob at Prineville had lynched five young men from Linn County for stealing horses. Portland dispatches spread the story to California and Nevada papers, but within days the Associated Press agent at The Dalles reported that no lynching had taken place, and the Albany paper that first printed the rumor declared it ill-founded.

episodes.title: Killing of Ed McElroy
episodes.summary: The killing of Ed McElroy took place at Frankfort, Kentucky, on the afternoon of August 7, 1882, a local election day, when a crowd at the polls shot dead McElroy, a Black man, after he fired a gun while officers tried to arrest him. The shot from McElroy's gun seriously wounded a man named Bud, or Sanford, Egbert. Telegraph dispatches carried the story across the country within days, most under headlines that cast McElroy as a "desperado" or "murderer."

episodes.title: Killing of John Wesley
episodes.summary: The killing of John Wesley was the shotgun murder of a well-to-do Black farmer at his home in southwestern Arkansas in the summer of 1882. Reports attributed the killing to young white men, and an attempt to arrest two suspects left a constable and two of his posse dead. Brothers named Coyle were later tried in Miller County circuit court, where the first defendant was acquitted and the charges against the others were dropped.

episodes.title: Attempted lynching of Riley Wiggins
episodes.summary: The attempted lynching of Riley Wiggins was an attempt in early August 1882 to lynch a Black hotel cook held in the jail at El Paso, Texas, after he killed two Mexicans who had shot him. Officials kept him safe, and the Dallas Daily Herald reported the case because Wiggins had been a well-known waiter at a Dallas hotel.

episodes.title: Hanging of Ben Holton
episodes.summary: The hanging of Ben Holton was a night attack in March 1882 in Oldham County, Kentucky, in which John and Alexander Duncan, wealthy distillers, hanged Holton, a Black man, by the neck three times to make him confess to burning their barn. Holton survived, and the attack became public only when he sued the brothers for $50,000 in the United States court at Louisville in July 1882. Papers across the country carried the suit as a curiosity, and in October Holton settled it for $700.

episodes.title: Threatened lynching of John Davis
episodes.doubt: friends lay in wait; no attack reported
episodes.summary: The threatened lynching of John Davis took place in Stamford in late July or early August 1882, when friends of women and girls he was accused of trying to assault lay in wait to lynch him. Officers arrested Davis and sent him to jail first, and a Connecticut weekly credited the arrest with preventing his death.

episodes.title: Killing of Henry Green
episodes.summary: The killing of Henry Green was the fatal shooting of a Black man by Deputy Sheriff T. G. Martin at Kyle, Texas, on Sunday, July 30, 1882, while Martin was trying to arrest him on a warrant. Green died the next day in the jail at San Marcos, and a coroner's jury found that he died of a shot fired by Martin, who was bound over to the district court.

episodes.title: Lynching of Henry Caldwell
episodes.summary: The lynching of Henry Caldwell took place early on July 30, 1882, when a masked mob took Caldwell, a Black man, from the Iron County jail at Ironton, Missouri, and hanged and shot him at a railroad bridge southeast of town. Caldwell had been bound over for trial on a charge of assaulting Mrs. Peck, a white woman of about sixty. The St. Louis wire spread the story nationally, some versions misplacing it at "Canton," while the local paper openly endorsed the killing.

episodes.title: Oatmanville shooting of Augustin Agirer
episodes.doubt: MWT lists Augustin Agirer (Mexican) as lynched, Oatmanville, Tex., 1882-08-15; our papers name two attackers (inventory disagreement: keep link, do not count).
episodes.summary: The Oatmanville shooting of Augustin Agirer was an attack on August 8, 1882, near Oatmanville in Travis County, Texas, in which two young white men shot Agirer and another Mexican, Redel, on the road home from a justice court where Agirer had won a complaint against their friend. Early reports said Agirer was killed, but an Austin dispatch the next day said both men were still alive and expected to die, and the shooters escaped arrest with help from friends.

episodes.title: Killing of Thomas Phearby
episodes.summary: The killing of Thomas Phearby took place on September 1, 1882, when Officer John Foster shot Phearby, a Black prisoner in his charge, in the woods about four miles from Spartanburg, South Carolina. A coroner's jury found that Phearby died from a pistol ball fired by Foster, and Foster was jailed.

episodes.title: Rape of Henrietta Robinson
episodes.summary: The rape of Henrietta Robinson was an assault on a Black woman by three white men, Maurice Connors, Patrick McNulty and James Reynolds, in the Swampoodle district of northeast Washington, D.C., in the early hours of September 3, 1882. Police arrested all three that night, and in November a jury convicted Connors of rape and found the other two guilty as accessories, a verdict the judge then set aside. The Washington dailies followed the case for nearly four months, and one paper's first headline said it was a case where "Judge Lynch" should have a say.

episodes.title: Helena election-day violence (1882)
episodes.summary: The Helena election-day violence took place at the Phillips County courthouse in Helena, Arkansas, on September 4, 1882, when Democrats and deputy sheriffs beat Republican ticket distributors and drove a crowd of about 1,000 Black voters from the polls. A deputy sheriff fired three times at a Black man, few Black men voted, and the Democrats claimed the county. Republican papers across the North treated the episode as the worst case of "bulldozing" in the state election, while Democratic papers dismissed it as invention.

episodes.title: Lynching of Winston Wade
episodes.summary: The lynching of Winston Wade took place at Union City, Tennessee, on the night of September 5, 1882, when a mob of about one hundred men took Wade, a Black man, from custody and hanged him to the limb of a tree. Wade had been accused of outraging Mrs. Sarah J. Young, a white woman, near the town three days earlier. A Nashville dispatch carried the story across the country within a day, and several papers printed it under headlines approving the hanging.

episodes.title: Attempted lynching of William Beaner
episodes.summary: The attempted lynching of William Beaner was a night ride by a party of horsemen on the Loudoun County jail at Leesburg, Virginia, on 7 September 1882, aimed at seizing and lynching a Black youth held there. The riders reached the jail, met the jailor and his sons, and turned back without trying to enter, and Beaner was not harmed. Local papers treated the failed raid with derision or, in one case, regret that the sheriff had been ready.

episodes.title: Lynching near Comanche, Texas (September 1882)
episodes.summary: The lynching near Comanche, Texas, was the killing in September 1882 of an unnamed Black man accused of raping a white girl, whom a posse pursued for ten miles, captured and lynched. The episode is known only from one-sentence telegraphic briefs that ran in papers from Tennessee to Dakota over the following two weeks.

episodes.title: Lynching of Gus Knight
episodes.summary: The lynching of Gus Knight was the killing of a Black man by a mob near Bartow, Jefferson County, Georgia, on September 11, 1882. Knight, accused of assaulting a married white woman that morning, was taken from two constables and shot. Georgia papers presented the killing as deserved vengeance, and a short wire telegram carried it to papers across the South and Midwest.

episodes.title: East St. Louis school dispute of 1882
episodes.summary: The East St. Louis school dispute of 1882 was a conflict in East St. Louis, Illinois, in September 1882, when Black children refused a separate school site were turned away from the white schools and street fights followed. The schools were closed on two successive days, and fights between white and Black children were reported before the dispute was said to have ended on September 13 with Black families accepting separate schools. Wire versions ran nationally under headlines such as "A War of Races" and "The Color Line."

episodes.title: Lynching of Nathan Bonnet
episodes.summary: The lynching of Nathan Bonnet took place at Williston, South Carolina, on the night of Wednesday, September 13, 1882, when a body of lynchers overpowered the jailer, took Bonnet, a Black prisoner, from the town jail, hanged him and riddled his body with bullets. Bonnet, described as seventeen years old, had been accused of entering a white man's house at midnight and attempting to rape his daughter, and was said to have confessed in jail. A short wire dispatch carried the story across the country within days, often under headlines approving the killing, while a South Carolina paper published a fuller account that praised it.

episodes.title: Shooting of a fleeing prisoner in Maysville, Kentucky (1882)
episodes.summary: The shooting of a fleeing prisoner in Maysville, Kentucky, took place on the night of September 19, 1882, when special policeman Fred. Bodie shot a Black man who had broken away from him after an arrest for obstructing the sidewalk. The man, whose name was not printed, was wounded in the hip, an injury the local paper described as slight.

episodes.title: Arnaudville night raid on Narcisse Semain's cabin
episodes.summary: The Arnaudville night raid on Narcisse Semain's cabin took place in September 1882, when an armed party of white men went at night to the home of Semain, a Black man living near Arnaudville, Louisiana, after a quarrel in the town. Semain shot and killed Marcellus Guitrot, a member of the party, and escaped. Local papers then disputed whether the men had come to punish him or as a constable's posse, and four of them were arrested on Semain's own affidavit.

episodes.title: Killing of John Spicy
episodes.summary: The killing of John Spicy was the fatal shooting of a Black man, also named in the papers as Lucius Edmunds, by men sent to arrest him at or near Leary's, Georgia, in late September 1882. The telegraphic dispatch from Atlanta described a fight with a sheriff's posse in which Spicy wounded one of the posse and accidentally shot his wife before he was killed. The brief dispatch ran in papers from Washington to Seattle, while a later Georgia account gave a different, longer sequence of events.

episodes.title: Lancaster riot of 1882
episodes.summary: The Lancaster riot of 1882 was a shooting on 27 September 1882 in the main street of Lancaster, South Carolina, in which armed white men killed at least four Black men from a mounted procession after a political meeting addressed by the Independent congressional candidate E. B. C. Cash. Reported deaths rose from four to as many as twelve, while no white man was said to have been seriously hurt. Southern Democratic papers called the shooting self-defense against a drunken mob, whereas Northern Republican voices called it a massacre and political murder.

episodes.title: Attempted lynching in Gonzales County, Texas (1882)
episodes.summary: The attempted lynching in Gonzales County, Texas, was the pursuit in late September 1882 of an unnamed Black prisoner, charged with assaulting a 12-year-old girl near Gonzales, by a mob reported at about 250 men. Officers moved him from jail to jail and finally by night and rail to San Antonio, where he was lodged safely in jail. The Dallas Herald told the story as a 'thrilling game of hide-and-seek' won by a state Ranger, Sergeant Rudd.

episodes.title: Dubuque jail attack on two Black roustabouts
episodes.summary: The Dubuque jail attack on two Black roustabouts was a beating of two Black prisoners by white fellow inmates in the jail at Dubuque, Iowa, in late summer 1882. The two men were struck with chair-rounds and table-legs until court-house officers stopped what the papers called a riot.
