Papers outside Iowa ran the item as an example of race prejudice in the North, describing it as 'an effort to draw the color line'.

episodes.title: Killing of Crockett Jenkins
episodes.summary: The killing of Crockett Jenkins was the hanging of a man described as a member of the Campbell gang, whose body was found on a hilltop oak near Princeton in Caldwell County, Kentucky, in late September 1882. One Kentucky paper called it another hanging by a mob, but the fuller accounts said suspicion fell on Mary Sullivan and female relatives, who were arrested and released. The case drew attention chiefly because Mary Sullivan was herself hanged by a mob from the same limb about a week later.

episodes.title: Lynching of Jim Rhodes
episodes.summary: The lynching of Jim Rhodes took place in the early morning of October 2, 1882, when masked, armed men took him from the jail at Charlottesville, Virginia, and hanged him from an oak tree on the Free Bridge road. Rhodes was awaiting trial for the axe murders of John O. Massie and his wife, an elderly Albemarle County couple, and the lynchers held off the commonwealth's attorney at gunpoint. Virginia papers disputed whether his last words were a confession and whether the jail's guards had been overpowered.

episodes.title: Attempted lynching of Robert Wilson
episodes.summary: The attempted lynching of Robert Wilson took place in Memphis, Tennessee, in the early hours of October 2, 1882, when a crowd of about 200 to 250 people gathered at the Shelby County jail and demanded Wilson, a 19-year-old Black prisoner accused of fatally shooting a grocer. The jailer refused to give up the keys and the crowd dispersed, and Wilson was later convicted of murder and sentenced to hang. Wire reports carried the story nationally as a failed lynching by a crowd that lacked a leader, while a Memphis daily openly regretted the failure.

episodes.title: Lynching of Henry Holloway
episodes.summary: The lynching of Henry Holloway took place on Tuesday, October 3, 1882, when a crowd seized Holloway, a young Black man accused of raping a white woman, at the end of a magistrates' hearing at Elkton in Giles County, Tennessee, and hanged him from the iron bridge over the Elk River. A short wire dispatch carried the story across the country within a day, and Tennessee papers openly approved the killing.

episodes.title: Lynching of John Brooks
episodes.summary: The lynching of John Brooks took place at Jacksonville, Alabama, on October 5, 1882, when a large crowd took Brooks, a Black prisoner, from the sheriff after his preliminary hearing and hanged him on the outskirts of the town. Brooks had been accused of assaulting a little girl near Anniston, and a wire dispatch from Anniston carried the story to dailies across the country.

episodes.title: Killing of Sid Dixon
episodes.summary: The killing of Sid Dixon was the fatal shooting of a Black mill hand by armed white pursuers in western Fulton County, Kentucky, near Hickman, in October 1882. After a week of quarrels, whites calling themselves a sheriff's posse hunted Dixon and other Black men; one report said Dixon was shot dead and two others wounded, while the local paper reported only wounds.

episodes.title: Killing of George Hathaway
episodes.summary: The killing of George Hathaway was the fatal shooting of a Black man by a white man, Martin Murphy, at a Black dance in Carlisle, Kentucky, on the night of September 27, 1882. Hathaway died on October 2, and Murphy escaped while armed men searched for him. A national wire brief retold the case as a white man defying a ban on white dancers, and it circulated from Delaware to Montana.

episodes.title: Killing of Daniel King at Kenner, Louisiana
episodes.summary: The killing of Daniel King was the fatal shooting of a drummer-boy at Kenner, Louisiana, on a Saturday evening in early October 1882, during the fall election season. The two surviving accounts disagree on who he was: a Mississippi weekly described a Black Democrat boy shot by a crowd of Black Republicans, while a wire brief called him a white drummer-boy killed in a political riot.

episodes.title: Shooting of Louis Guilford
episodes.summary: The shooting of Louis Guilford took place at Tarboro, North Carolina, on October 23, 1882, when Guilford, a Black man under arrest, was shot and mortally wounded by men who pursued and recaptured him after he escaped. According to the dispatch, Guilford had cut the arresting constable with a razor and wounded two of his captors, and papers across the country ran the story as the act of a "fighting" or "murderous" Black man.

episodes.title: Attempted lynching of Riley Anderson (October 1882)
episodes.summary: The attempted lynching of Riley Anderson was a night raid on the Greenville County jail in Greenville, South Carolina, on October 2, 1882, by a party of white and Black men seeking to hang Anderson, a Black man accused of murdering a woman and her infant. Warned in advance, Sheriff Gilreath had already hidden Anderson, and the crowd dispersed after the sheriff spoke to it. South Carolina papers carried the story chiefly from the Greenville News, dwelling on the sheriff's stratagem.

episodes.title: Lynching of Bill Harris
episodes.summary: The lynching of Bill Harris was the shooting of a Black man by a pursuing mob at his wife's house in Bastrop parish, Louisiana, around November 1, 1882. Harris was accused of attacking the young daughter of a white planter named Wilder, and the party that captured him fired twenty guns at him at once. The story reached papers across the country through a Shreveport wire dispatch under headlines such as "Twenty Shots at One Man."

episodes.title: Ashland mob attack on the Granite State (1882)
episodes.summary: The Ashland mob attack on the Granite State took place on November 1, 1882, when a mob at Ashland, Kentucky, tried to seize William Neal and Ellis Craft, prisoners accused of murder, from State Guard troops carrying them down the Ohio River. The troops fired on the mob's ferryboat and on the crowd watching from the bank, killing five or six townspeople, while the prisoners reached jail unharmed. A coroner's jury held the troops' commander culpable for the killings.

episodes.title: Lynching of Andrew Jackson
episodes.summary: The lynching of Andrew Jackson was the killing of a Black man by a mob in early November 1882, reported as having taken place near Vienna, in Lincoln Parish, Louisiana. Jackson was accused of assaulting a white girl, whom one report described as eight years old. The killing reached national readers only as a one-sentence item, first under a Vicksburg, Mississippi, dateline and then in weekly news-brief columns.

episodes.title: Manhunt and shooting of Wesley Fisher
episodes.summary: The manhunt and shooting of Wesley Fisher took place near Cumberland, Maryland, in late October and early November 1882, when Fisher, a young Black man accused of raping a farmer's wife, was hunted by armed citizens and shot by two private captors on November 3. He survived his wounds and was jailed amid threats of lynching, which the sheriff was reported determined to resist. Fisher denied the charge, was identified by the woman at a hearing, and was held for the grand jury.

episodes.title: Nashville streetcar riot (1882)
episodes.summary: The Nashville streetcar riot took place on the night of November 6, 1882, when a Black crowd at a Republican rally on Cherry street in Nashville, Tennessee, seized the driver of a streetcar that had run over and killed an elderly Black man, Alfred King, and tried to lynch him. Police and a constable got the wounded driver, Benjamin Woodward, to jail, which citizens and soldiers then guarded against the crowd.

episodes.title: Vienna, Louisiana, jail lynching (1882)
episodes.summary: The Vienna, Louisiana, jail lynching took place on the night of November 6, 1882, when a group of men forced the jail at Vienna and took out four Black prisoners who had been sent there from Jackson parish for safekeeping. Two of the prisoners, charged with robbing and trying to kill an elderly white man named Ray, were found the next morning shot to death outside town, while one escaped and another was reportedly spared. An Associated Press dispatch carried the story to papers across the country, and Louisiana papers followed with their own notices.

episodes.title: Rockingham registration fight (1882)
episodes.summary: The Rockingham registration fight was an attack by a large party of white men on a revenue officer named Spears and about 100 Black men he had brought to register as voters at Rockingham, North Carolina, on election day, November 7, 1882. Spears was badly beaten and several of the Black men were severely injured, and many arrests were reported.

episodes.title: Florence election riot (1882)
episodes.summary: The Florence election riot was an attack on Black voters at the polls at or near Florence, South Carolina, on election day, November 7, 1882, in which two or three "colored men" were shot and the election there was broken up. The news came chiefly from a telegram by E. H. Deas, the Republican candidate for Congress in the Sixth District, who said the men were shot for insisting on voting the Republican ticket. Wire reports turned his account into two or three killed, and Republican papers in the North cited it as an example of Democratic intimidation.

episodes.title: Killing of Israel Groff
episodes.summary: The killing of Israel Groff took place on November 7, 1882, election day, when Frederick, Maryland, policeman Porter shot Groff, a Black man, dead during a fight at a city polling precinct. A crowd that the National Republican put at several hundred Black men then surrounded the house of Judge John A. Lynch, where the officer had taken refuge, and threatened to lynch him before he was taken to jail. Porter was released on bail eleven days later, and accounts of why he fired differed sharply.

episodes.title: Wilmington Third Ward election riot
episodes.summary: The Wilmington Third Ward election riot was a fight between a white crowd and a party of Black men near the Third Ward polls in Wilmington, Delaware, on the afternoon of election day, November 7, 1882. Several men in the crowd were shot, a Black man named Lewis Woodland had his skull fractured by a stone, and three Black men were later charged with riot. The local Republican paper said the whites began the fight, while the Associated Press dispatch printed across the country called the Black men the assailants.

episodes.title: Killing of Jack Hendricks
episodes.summary: The killing of Jack Hendricks was the fatal shooting of a Black man by Constable Wright in Campbell County, Virginia, near Lynchburg, on November 9, 1882. Hendricks was under arrest for "malicious cutting," and the only published account, a brief Lynchburg dispatch, said he was shot while trying to escape. The dispatch ran the next day in papers from Richmond to Dallas and St. Paul, usually as a single line among other news.

episodes.title: Lynching of Counce O'Neal
episodes.summary: The lynching of Counce O'Neal was the killing of a Black man near Dublin, Georgia, in late November 1882, when a group of men took him from his house at night and riddled his body with bullets. A Macon dispatch said he had been killed for an alleged assault on a little girl and was afterward found to be innocent, while other reports blamed Black neighbors with a grudge.

episodes.title: Killing of Julius Hurt
episodes.summary: The killing of Julius Hurt was the fatal shooting of a Black man by a local officer, William Jones, at Campbellsville, Kentucky, on November 27, 1882. Jones said Hurt had resisted arrest on a bench warrant, and he was acquitted at an examining trial the same day. A short dispatch about the killing ran in papers from Washington to California, one of which counted it as Kentucky's "daily murder."

episodes.title: Killing of Joe Ross
episodes.summary: The killing of Joe Ross was the fatal shooting of a Black man, known in Camden, South Carolina, as Joe Wilson, by ferryman Alonzo Huntley at Ivey's Mill on the Catawba River in Lancaster County on the night of December 6, 1882. Ross was accused of killing F. M. McDowell, a white Camden man, with an axe on Thanksgiving morning, and he was shot while fleeing a citizens' party from Camden that was described as 'bent on lynching him' and that had posted the ferryman. He died the next morning after giving what the papers called a confession, and his death was reported by wire across the country.

episodes.title: Setauket rubber factory riot
episodes.summary: The Setauket rubber factory riot was an attack in late October or early November 1882 by Irish and other white residents of Setauket, Long Island, New York, on the town's Black residents, who, like the Irish, had recently come there in large numbers to work in the rubber factory. After a white man was reported beaten by Black men, whites beat every Black man they found on the streets and attacked Black homes until armed Black residents drove them off. No deaths were reported, and the story ran nationally as a race feud under headings such as "An Irish-African Feud" and "A War of Races."

episodes.title: Shooting of Hicks by Constable King
episodes.summary: The shooting of Hicks by Constable King took place in Sampson County, North Carolina, in late November 1882, when a constable serving an arrest warrant seriously wounded Hicks, a Black schoolteacher. The only surviving report, a brief item from the Clinton Caucasian reprinted in Raleigh, said that Hicks had resisted the officer with an axe.

episodes.title: Shooting of Hannibal Lee
episodes.summary: The shooting of Hannibal Lee was the wounding of a Black man by Town Marshal Jim Walker in Pineville, Louisiana, on Saturday, December 2, 1882. Lee was reported "dangerously wounded," and the only surviving report justified the shooting by saying he had resisted arrest and assaulted the marshal.

episodes.title: Killing of Bill Allen
episodes.summary: The killing of Bill Allen was the shooting by Chicago police of a Black waiter in a chicken coop near the North Halsted Street rail yards on Sunday afternoon, December 3, 1882, after a city-wide manhunt. Allen was accused of killing Officer Clarence E. Wright four days earlier, and the most widely printed dispatch said police shot him after he threw up his hands and offered to surrender. A crowd of thousands then tried to hang his body, and a coroner's jury exonerated the two officers who shot him.

episodes.title: Sedalia police shooting of 1882
episodes.summary: The Sedalia police shooting of 1882 was an incident in Sedalia, Missouri, probably on the afternoon of 4 December 1882, in which Officer Wentzelman clubbed an unnamed Black man he had arrested and then fired three pistol shots at him as he fled. None of the shots hit him, and the man escaped. The only known account is a short local item in the Sedalia Weekly Bazoo, told from the officer's side.

episodes.title: Attempted lynching of the Lebanon Cemetery body snatchers
episodes.summary: The attempted lynching of the Lebanon Cemetery body snatchers took place in Philadelphia on December 5, 1882, when a crowd of Black residents outside a magistrate's office threatened to lynch four men charged with stealing bodies from a Black burial ground. Police held off two rushes and took the prisoners to the Central station, and the wire carried the story under headlines such as "The Ghouls Nearly Lynched."

episodes.title: Lynching of Tom Robinson and Bill Cephas
episodes.summary: The lynching of Tom Robinson and Bill Cephas took place at Bastrop, in Morehouse Parish, Louisiana, in early December 1882, when a body of men broke open the jail and hanged the two Black prisoners from a tree near the town. The two men were being held on a charge of shooting a young white man named Curry, who survived. The wire account, which said local opinion sided with the lynchers and blamed 'indulgent juries', ran in papers from Maine to California.

episodes.title: Killing of Joe Ross
episodes.summary: The killing of Joe Ross was the fatal shooting of Joe Ross, a Black man also known as Joe Wilson, by ferryman Alonzo Huntley at Ivy's Mill on the Catawba River in Lancaster County, South Carolina, on the night of December 6, 1882. Ross was being hunted by a party of Camden citizens as the accused killer of F. N. McDowell, and they had posted the ferryman at the crossing. Wire services carried the news across the country, and North Carolina papers hailed it as revenge for two killings Ross was said to have confessed.

episodes.title: Killing of Joe Walker
episodes.summary: The killing of Joe Walker took place at Skipwith, Mississippi, on the night of Saturday, December 9, 1882, when constable J. A. Lawson shot Walker, a Black man, while trying to arrest him for gambling. Walker died of the wound two days later, and Lawson was arrested and released on bail. The only account, a dispatch from Skipwith giving the constable's side, ran as a short crime item in papers from Mississippi to Minnesota.

episodes.title: Threatened lynching of Lockie at Thomson, Georgia
episodes.summary: The threatened lynching of Lockie at Thomson, Georgia, took place after John L. Cushion was shot and killed there on the night of December 10, 1882, and a Black man named Lockie was arrested on suspicion. According to an Augusta dispatch, "the people" were restrained "with great difficulty" from lynching him, and no killing of the accused was reported. The story ran as a one-sentence wire item in December 1882 and was carried into weekly news digests later that month.

episodes.title: Oconee riot of 1882
episodes.summary: The Oconee riot of 1882 was a gun and knife fight at Oconee, Georgia, on Christmas Day, Dec. 25, 1882, in which the town marshal, his son, the mayor and white citizens shot several Black men who resisted an arrest. Three or four Black men were wounded, one of them reported likely to die, and the marshal and his son were also hurt. Georgia and national papers called it a 'riot' and a 'race riot', but their counts of the dead and wounded differed widely.

episodes.title: Killing of Charles Smith (Waxahachie, 1882)
episodes.summary: The killing of Charles Smith was the shooting of a Black man by a posse of armed citizens at Waxahachie, Texas, in December 1882, shortly after he was said to have shot and killed City Marshal J. H. Spalding, who was trying to arrest him. Cornered in a privy about an hour after the marshal's death, Smith was 'riddled with bullets', and a coroner's jury attributed his death to unknown parties summoned by the sheriff. The story circulated nationally as a brief wire item in which the marshal's 'murderer' met a swift end.

episodes.title: Lynching of an unnamed Black man near Millen, Georgia (1882)
episodes.summary: The lynching of an unnamed Black man near Millen, Georgia, took place in December 1882, when a mob overpowered the posse taking him to jail and killed him. He had been accused of attempting to assault a young white woman and had been bound over for trial. A Waynesboro letter in the Savannah Morning News and an Augusta wire dispatch reported the killing, and the wire carried it to papers across the country under headings such as "Lynch Law in Georgia."

episodes.title: Killing of John Franklin
episodes.summary: The killing of John Franklin was the fatal shooting of a Black prisoner by City Marshal John Way in a cell of the jail at South Charleston, Ohio, on the night of December 25, 1882. Way said Franklin attacked him when he entered the cell, and that account, from a single dispatch, was printed across the country among the season's 'Christmas crimes'.

episodes.title: Atlanta Christmas police shooting (1882)
episodes.summary: The Atlanta Christmas police shooting was the wounding of an unnamed Black man by an Atlanta policeman, who shot him in the leg on Christmas Day, 1882. The only reason given was that the man had tried to take the officer's club, and the shooting reached northern papers as one line in a wire list of Atlanta's Christmas "casualties."

episodes.title: Lynching of Charley Branch
episodes.summary: The lynching of Charley Branch took place late on the night of Tuesday, December 26, 1882, near Varner Station, Arkansas, when an armed mob took Branch, a Black man, from his guards and hanged him to a telegraph pole. Branch had been arrested two days earlier, accused of ravishing and murdering a nine-year-old girl. A short Little Rock wire dispatch carried the news across the country, and several papers headlined it with approval, the Omaha Daily Bee calling it "A Deed to Applaud."

episodes.title: Oconee Christmas Day riot
episodes.summary: The Oconee Christmas Day riot was an armed clash on December 25, 1882, at Oconee, Georgia, between the town marshal, the mayor and white citizens and a group of Black men the marshal was trying to arrest. Three or four Black men were shot, one reportedly mortally, and the marshal and his son were wounded. A Macon wire sent across the country on December 30 called it a "race riot" that had killed a white man, but a second Macon dispatch the same day said no one had been killed.

episodes.title: Lincolnton riot arrests and banishment (1882)
episodes.summary: The Lincolnton riot arrests and banishment took place in Lincolnton, North Carolina, in December 1882, when thirty Black men were jailed for a riot and, after trial, all but one were acquitted on condition that they leave the town. Wire reports of armed patrols, threats to burn the town and troops ordered to the scene spread nationally before dispatches from Charlotte and Lincolnton denied that any renewed trouble had occurred.

episodes.title: Killing of Henry Herndon
episodes.summary: The killing of Henry Herndon was the fatal shooting of a Black man, described as "colored," by James Dameron, a policeman, at Springfield, Missouri, in late 1882. It is known only from a one-line item in a Kentucky paper's news column, which attributed the shooting to "an old grudge."

episodes.title: Lynching near Millen, Georgia (1882)
episodes.summary: The lynching near Millen, Georgia, was the killing in December 1882 of an unnamed Black man whom a mob took from the officers escorting him to jail. He had been arrested and bound over for trial on a charge of attempting to outrage a young white woman. An Augusta wire dispatch carried the case to papers across the country, where shortened copies misnamed the place as "Nelson" or "Wilton."

episodes.title: Lynching of James Carroll
episodes.summary: The lynching of James Carroll took place on the evening of April 17, 1879, near Point of Rocks, Frederick County, Maryland, when a crowd took Carroll, a young Black man, from two Washington policemen on a Baltimore and Ohio train and hanged him from a tree. Carroll had been arrested in Georgetown that day, accused of an 'outrage' on Mrs. Richard Thomas of Licksville, and was being taken to Frederick for trial. Two Evening Star reporters rode the train and described the seizure, and a coroner's jury found that he had been 'unlawfully hanged' by men unknown.

episodes.title: Lynching of an unnamed prisoner at Starke, Florida
episodes.summary: The lynching of an unnamed prisoner at Starke, Florida, took place in Bradford County some time before early October 1882, when lynchers broke open the county jail and hanged a Black man held on a charge of assaulting a young woman. The only account is a short item in the Starke Weekly Telegraph, known from a reprint in the Savannah Morning News, and a Tallahassee editorial later listed the killing among Florida crimes whose perpetrators were still unpunished.

episodes.title: Whipping of Bibb County chain gang convicts
episodes.summary: The whipping of Bibb County chain gang convicts was the beating of two Black convicts by a guard of the county chain gang in Bibb County, Georgia, reported in November 1882. The Bibb County grand jury proposed to investigate the case, and within days the county's Road Commissioners gave up control of the chain gang to the County Commissioners.

episodes.title: Troy depot crowd incident
episodes.summary: The Troy depot crowd incident was a confrontation at the railway depot in Troy, Pennsylvania, about August 25, 1882, in which a crowd shouted threats at a Black man boarding a night train with a white woman. Told that the pair were eloping, the crowd cried "Hang the man," and the man left the train; no one was reported hurt.

episodes.title: Killing of Gray in Hawkins County, Tennessee
episodes.summary: The killing of Gray took place in December 1882 in the mountainous part of Hawkins County, Tennessee, when a party of white men came to his cabin at night to whip him over an accusation that he had stolen hogs. In the gunfire that followed, Gray, a Black man, was mortally wounded and died, his stepson's thigh was broken, and two of the white men were wounded. A Knoxville dispatch describing it as a "terrible tragedy" ran in papers across the country.
